abstract: This brief essay argues that computational communication research has entered a 'post-API age' following Facebook's April 2018 closure of its Pages API, which eliminated all terms-of-service-compliant methods for extracting Facebook content. Freelon contends that heavy investment in platform-specific API methods is dangerously fragile, since companies can restrict or eliminate access at any time without recourse. He offers two guiding recommendations for graduate education in computational methods: learning web scraping as a more robust skill, and understanding the legal and ethical consequences of violating platforms' terms of service.
key_claims: The closure of Facebook's Pages API in April 2018 marks a shift into a 'post-API age' in which there is no TOS-compliant way to independently extract Facebook content.
Reliance on APIs alone is risky because access can be restricted or eliminated overnight, rendering platform-specific methods and training obsolete.
Web scraping is a more flexible and durable research skill than API extraction, though it is harder to learn and often raises legal and ethical concerns.
TOS compliance is distinct from human subjects compliance and privacy protection: respecting a company's terms does not equate to protecting users.
Researchers must weigh the risks—technical, legal, and ethical—of violating platform TOS when authorized methods are unavailable.
methods: Reflective/argumentative essay rather than an empirical study.
Draws on the author's own experience (a Facebook data collection workshop and a Python module for the Pages API that were rendered obsolete).

Reviews and compares web scraping tools: browser extensions (Web Scraper, Grepsr), standalone software (Teleport Pro), cloud solutions (Import.io, Webhose.io), and code-based frameworks (BeautifulSoup, Selenium).
Uses illustrative cases such as collecting US Congressional campaign messages via Twitter API versus scraping candidate websites.
findings: Code-based scraping tools like BeautifulSoup and Selenium offer maximum flexibility at minimum cost but require understanding each target page's unique DOM structure, making them harder to learn and site-specific.
Many major platforms (Facebook, Google) prohibit automated scraping in their TOS and attempt to detect and block it, though carefully crafted software can circumvent restrictions.

Consequences of TOS violation range from blacklisted API credentials and temporary IP bans to, in extreme cases, criminal prosecution under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (as in the Aaron Swartz case).
The pending Sandvig v. Sessions lawsuit challenges the practice of criminally prosecuting TOS violations, but its unresolved status leaves researchers uncertain.
contributions: Names and diagnoses the 'post-API age' as a defining challenge for computational communication research.
Provides practical guidance for graduate computational methods curricula, advocating web scraping instruction alongside APIs.
Articulates a set of ethical/legal recommendations: use authorized methods when possible, distinguish TOS compliance from research ethics, and understand the risks of TOS violation.
Calls on scholars to prioritize data-access fragility in future publications and conference submissions.
framing: The essay is positioned within computational and social media research methodology, engaging debates over data access, research ethics, platform governance, and the tension between corporate terms of service and scholarly needs. It frames data access as inherently tenuous and contingent on corporate power, urging methodological resilience and ethical reflexivity.
